A request at your own library can send a book traveling between shared shelves. I like a reading adventure that begins close to home. ♡

blocks.text: There’s a book I’d like to look for with you: a history of Cincinnati’s Findlay Market. It might take a little trip through Ohio before it reaches your pickup shelf. Your part can start right at your own library’s catalog. Shall we follow the request? I’m already looking forward to the reading part. ♡

Here’s our title: Alyssa McClanahan’s Findlay Market of Cincinnati: A History, published by Arcadia in 2021, ISBN 9781467148597. SearchOhio and OhioLINK connect participating collections through local public-library catalogs. The request begins with your own library and ends at a chosen pickup desk. I like that the book can do the traveling while your starting point stays close to home.

blocks.title: Begin where your card works
blocks.eyebrow: One title, several ways to search

blocks.text: I’d start with the catalog linked by the library that issued your card. Try the title, author, or ISBN, then check the edition, format, owning library, and current availability. One important change: OhioLINK’s standalone Central Catalog stopped operating on June 26, 2025; its shared collections are now reached through local catalogs. An old bookmark might be sending you the long way around. Let’s give the local catalog first try.

steps.title: Find the record
steps.text: Search the title, author, or ISBN in your own library catalog and review the edition and format.

steps.title: Request it
steps.text: If the record offers SearchOhio or OhioLINK, choose its request control, select your affiliated library, enter the requested account details, and choose a pickup location.

steps.title: Wait for notice
steps.text: SearchOhio says requests are usually ready within 3–5 business days, excluding weekend requests; that is an estimate, not a delivery promise.

steps.title: Pick up and return
steps.text: Collect the item after the library notifies you. Follow the owning and pickup library’s rules for due dates, renewals, fees, and eligible return locations.

blocks.text: Your arrival notice tells you when to collect the book; your account gives the due date. That’s the point where I’d allow myself a little “yay!” and start choosing a reading spot. A window seat would tempt me. ♡
blocks.title: Wait for the pickup notice

blocks.text: Found a request option? SearchOhio’s instructions say to choose your affiliated library, sign in with your last name and card number—and a PIN where required—then select a pickup point. It lists a usual arrival time of three to five business days, except for weekend requests, and a ten-day pickup hold. That’s an estimate: the title might be unavailable, non-circulating, or already requested. I’d wait for the arrival notice before making a special trip. The cheerful part is much nicer when the book is actually there.

blocks.title: The local library still sets important terms
blocks.eyebrow: Check the account that will receive the item

blocks.text: Here’s where I’d keep your own library’s page open. Columbus Metropolitan Library lists 21-day loans for print, audiobooks, and music, seven days for movies, and up to three renewals if nobody else is waiting. It lists a ten-day pickup hold and separate fee and replacement policies for SearchOhio and OhioLINK items. Those are Columbus terms. Another library can have different rules, so follow its guidance and the due date in your account.

No request button? Mm, I wouldn’t give up on the title just yet. OhioLINK’s FAQ directs questions about requests and fines to your local library. The item and your participating library determine what’s available; a librarian may be able to find another edition or another interlibrary-loan route. That’s a good question to bring to a person rather than keep asking the same search box.

blocks.title: Let the book lead back to the market

blocks.text: Once the book arrives, I’d follow one detail toward the real market. Findlay’s own history dates its iron-framed building to 1852 and its opening to 1855 after construction disputes and difficulties with the method. Then come the tower, enclosure, plumbing, and refrigeration. Ooh, a whole building changing around everyday shopping. The catalog tells us which edition we have; the book and the market’s account give us different ways into the past.

We can keep your part of the journey small: one title, your account, a pickup point that suits you, and a return following your library’s instructions. Search first, request when the active record offers it, then wait for the notice. I’m fond of how much shared work sits behind such an ordinary little errand.
One book, one pickup notice, a little time together with the pages. Ahh, that sounds like a very good afternoon to me. ♡
